anchor.title: President Truman Signing the Document Implementing the North Atlantic Treaty, Oval Office (1949)
anchor.creator: Abbie Rowe / National Park Service / Harry S. Truman Library; National Archives and Records Administration
anchor.citation: Rowe, Abbie. "Photograph of President Truman Signing the Document Implementing the North Atlantic Treaty at His Desk in the Oval Office." 1949. Harry S. Truman Library / National Archives and Records Administration (NAID 200163), via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Photograph_of_President_Truman_signing_the_document_implementing_the_North_Atlantic_Treaty_at_his_desk_in_the_Oval..._-_NARA_-_200163.jpg.
anchor.alt: Black-and-white photograph of President Harry S. Truman seated at his Oval Office desk, signing the document implementing the North Atlantic Treaty on August 24, 1949, while officials and diplomats stand behind him.
anchor.caption: This photograph shows President Truman signing the document that put the North Atlantic Treaty into effect in 1949, creating NATO — a military alliance among the United States, Canada, and ten Western European nations. The treaty's most important provision, Article 5, declared that an attack on any member nation would be treated as an attack on all of them, requiring a collective response. The signing marked a revolution in American foreign policy: for the first time in peacetime, the United States committed itself to the permanent defense of Europe. Truman's decision to create NATO reflected the lesson American leaders had learned from World War II — that staying out of European conflicts did not keep America safe. By forming a permanent alliance, the United States signaled to the Soviet Union that any westward expansion would meet unified military resistance.

anchor.title: C-47s at Tempelhof Airport, Berlin, During the Berlin Airlift (1948)
anchor.creator: U.S. Air Force / U.S. Federal Government
anchor.citation: U.S. Air Force. "C-47s at Tempelhof Airport, Berlin, During the Berlin Airlift." 1948. U.S. Air Force, via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:C-47s_at_Tempelhof_Airport_Berlin_1948.jpg.
anchor.alt: Black-and-white photograph of multiple C-47 Skytrain transport aircraft parked on the tarmac at Tempelhof Airport in West Berlin, Germany, during the Berlin Airlift of 1948–1949.
anchor.caption: This photograph shows American C-47 transport aircraft at Berlin's Tempelhof Airport during the Berlin Airlift of 1948–1949. After the Soviet Union blocked all road, rail, and canal routes into the Western sectors of Berlin in June 1948, the United States and Britain responded by flying in all the supplies needed to keep 2.5 million West Berliners alive. At the height of the operation, a plane landed every three minutes, day and night. Over 462 days, Western planes made more than 200,000 flights and delivered 2.3 million tons of food, coal, and supplies. The Soviets lifted the blockade in May 1949, and the airlift became one of the first major Western victories of the Cold War — proving that the United States would resist Soviet pressure without firing a shot.

anchor.title: Senator Joseph R. McCarthy (c. 1954)
anchor.creator: United Press / U.S. Senate (public record portrait)
anchor.citation: United Press. "Senator Joseph R. McCarthy." c. 1954. Via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Joseph_McCarthy_adjusted.jpg.
anchor.alt: Black-and-white portrait photograph of Senator Joseph R. McCarthy of Wisconsin, seated, facing slightly to his right, c. 1954.
anchor.caption: This photograph shows Senator Joseph McCarthy of Wisconsin, the most prominent figure of the Second Red Scare — a period of intense fear about communist spies and subversion in the United States during the late 1940s and early 1950s. Beginning in 1950, McCarthy claimed to have lists of communists working inside the U.S. government, and his Senate investigations destroyed the careers of hundreds of Americans through accusations that were often unsupported by evidence. 'McCarthyism' became a term for the dangerous practice of making political accusations without proof. The Army-McCarthy hearings in 1954, watched by millions on television, finally exposed McCarthy's recklessness. The Senate censured him in December 1954, ending his power — but by then, McCarthyism had demonstrated how Cold War fear could be exploited to threaten civil liberties.

anchor.title: Battle of Inchon, Korean War (September 1950)
anchor.creator: U.S. military / U.S. Federal Government
anchor.citation: U.S. military. "Battle of Inchon, Korean War." Sept. 1950. U.S. Department of Defense / National Archives and Records Administration, via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Battle_of_Inchon.png.
anchor.alt: Black-and-white photograph of U.S. Marines landing at Inchon during the Korean War amphibious assault in September 1950, with landing craft and troops visible on the beach.
anchor.caption: This photograph documents the amphibious landing at Inchon, South Korea, on September 15, 1950 — one of the most brilliant military operations of the Korean War. General Douglas MacArthur planned a daring attack by sea at a location most experts considered too dangerous because of its extreme tidal conditions. The operation succeeded brilliantly: U.S. and U.N. forces outflanked North Korean armies that had nearly conquered all of South Korea, recaptured the capital Seoul within two weeks, and reversed the entire war. The victory made MacArthur a national hero. But when he pushed north toward China's border against Truman's warnings, China sent 300,000 troops into the war in November 1950. The war was transformed from a likely United Nations victory into a bloody stalemate that would last until 1953. MacArthur's public disagreement with Truman's strategy led Truman to fire him in April 1951, raising a fundamental question about civilian control of the military in a democracy.

anchor.title: Dwight D. Eisenhower, Official Photo Portrait (May 29, 1959)
anchor.creator: White House / U.S. Federal Government
anchor.citation: White House. "Dwight D. Eisenhower, Official Photo Portrait." 29 May 1959. Via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Dwight_D._Eisenhower,_official_photo_portrait,_May_29,_1959.jpg.
anchor.alt: Official color White House portrait photograph of President Dwight D. Eisenhower, facing slightly left, wearing a dark suit and tie, May 29, 1959.
anchor.caption: This official White House portrait shows President Dwight D. Eisenhower, a former five-star general who commanded the Allied forces in World War II and then served as president from 1953 to 1961. As president, Eisenhower shaped Cold War strategy through his 'New Look' defense policy, which relied on nuclear weapons and air power rather than expensive conventional armies — a strategy called 'massive retaliation.' He ended the Korean War in 1953 and navigated multiple Cold War crises. His farewell address in January 1961 is famous for warning Americans about the growing power of the 'military-industrial complex' — the dangerous alliance between defense contractors and military leaders who benefited financially from a permanent state of high defense spending. Eisenhower's warning proved remarkably prescient as the Cold War continued and U.S. defense budgets remained enormous for decades.

anchor.title: Operation Upshot-Knothole, 'Badger' Atomic Test, Nevada Test Site (April 18, 1953)
anchor.creator: National Nuclear Security Administration / Nevada Site Office / U.S. Federal Government
anchor.citation: National Nuclear Security Administration. "Operation Upshot-Knothole, 'Badger' Atomic Test, Nevada Test Site." 18 Apr. 1953. U.S. Department of Energy, via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Operation_Upshot-Knothole_-_Badger_001.jpg.
anchor.alt: Color photograph of the 'Badger' nuclear weapons test detonation at the Nevada Test Site on April 18, 1953, showing a large mushroom cloud rising over the desert with the fireball still visible at the base.
anchor.caption: This photograph shows a nuclear weapons test explosion at the Nevada Test Site on April 18, 1953 — part of the U.S. effort to develop and improve nuclear weapons during the Cold War arms race. Between 1951 and 1962, the United States conducted 100 above-ground nuclear tests in Nevada. These tests were driven by Cold War competition with the Soviet Union, which had tested its first atomic bomb in 1949 and first hydrogen bomb just months before this photograph was taken. The arms race created a condition called Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD): both superpowers had so many nuclear weapons that any all-out nuclear war would destroy both countries. The testing program also had serious environmental and public health consequences: radioactive fallout from Nevada tests drifted across the American West, exposing thousands of civilians — especially downwind communities in Utah and Nevada — to dangerous levels of radiation, causing elevated cancer rates that Congress finally acknowledged in 1990.

anchor.title: Aerial Photograph of Medium Range Ballistic Missile Launch Site Two at San Cristobal, Cuba (October 1962)
anchor.creator: U.S. Air Force / Central Intelligence Agency reconnaissance; National Archives and Records Administration
anchor.citation: U.S. Air Force. "Aerial Photograph of Medium Range Ballistic Missile Launch Site Two at San Cristobal, Cuba." Oct. 1962. National Archives and Records Administration (NAID 193933), via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Aerial_Photograph_of_Medium_Range_Ballistic_Missile_Launch_Site_Two_at_San_Cristobal_-_NARA_-_193933.tif.
anchor.alt: Black-and-white U.S. Air Force aerial reconnaissance photograph of a Soviet medium-range ballistic missile launch site under construction at San Cristóbal, Cuba, with labels indicating missile erectors, launch pads, and missile-ready tents, October 1962.
anchor.caption: This aerial reconnaissance photograph, taken by a U.S. spy plane over Cuba in October 1962, shows a Soviet nuclear missile launch site under construction near San Cristóbal, Cuba. When CIA analysts showed photographs like this to President Kennedy on October 16, 1962, they triggered the Cuban Missile Crisis — the most dangerous confrontation of the Cold War. Soviet medium-range ballistic missiles in Cuba could have hit most U.S. cities within five minutes. For thirteen days, the United States and Soviet Union stood at the brink of nuclear war. Kennedy chose a naval quarantine and secret diplomacy rather than military strikes. The crisis was resolved when Soviet Premier Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles in exchange for a U.S. promise not to invade Cuba and a secret U.S. agreement to remove its own Jupiter missiles from Turkey. The crisis led both sides to establish the Moscow-Washington hotline and eventually negotiate arms control agreements.

anchor.title: 1st Cavalry Division (Airmobile) Soldiers Wait for a Helicopter at an LZ, Vietnam War
anchor.creator: U.S. Army / U.S. Federal Government
anchor.citation: U.S. Army. "1st Cavalry Division (Airmobile) Soldiers Wait for a Helicopter to Land at an LZ." c. 1966–1968. U.S. Army, via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:1st_Cavalry_Division,_(Airmobile)_soldiers_wait_for_a_helicopter_to_land_at_an_LZ.jpg.
anchor.alt: Color photograph of U.S. Army soldiers from the 1st Cavalry Division (Airmobile) crouching in grass and waiting for a UH-1 Huey helicopter to land at a landing zone during the Vietnam War, circa 1966–1968.
anchor.caption: This photograph shows American soldiers from the 1st Cavalry Division waiting for a Huey helicopter during the Vietnam War. Helicopters were the defining technology of the Vietnam War — used to move troops rapidly through jungle terrain where roads didn't exist, evacuate wounded soldiers, and provide close air support. The U.S. military deployed cutting-edge technology and enormous firepower in Vietnam, but faced a guerrilla war against North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces that used tunnels, jungle cover, and popular support to offset American technological advantages. Despite deploying over 500,000 troops and conducting more than 1 million helicopter sorties per year by 1968, the United States could not achieve a decisive military victory. The inability to translate military operations like the one shown in this photograph into lasting political gains contributed to growing public opposition at home and eventually to the withdrawal of American forces from Vietnam.

anchor.title: Vietnam War Protesters at the March on the Pentagon (October 21, 1967)
anchor.creator: U.S. Department of Defense / Frank Wolfe (U.S. Federal Government)
anchor.citation: U.S. Department of Defense. "Vietnam War Protesters at the March on the Pentagon." 21 Oct. 1967. National Archives, via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vietnam_War_protestors_at_the_March_on_the_Pentagon.jpg.
anchor.alt: Black-and-white photograph of Vietnam War protesters gathered at the March on the Pentagon on October 21, 1967, with a large crowd visible and the Pentagon building in the background.
anchor.caption: This photograph documents the March on the Pentagon on October 21, 1967, when approximately 100,000 anti-Vietnam War protesters gathered in Washington, D.C. By 1967, over 15,000 American soldiers had died in Vietnam, and a growing anti-war movement was challenging the Johnson administration's claim that the war was being won. The protest movement united students, civil rights activists, veterans, and ordinary citizens frustrated by the war's mounting costs and unclear objectives. The March on the Pentagon — in which some protesters tried to literally surround and occupy the Department of Defense — marked a new level of confrontation between the anti-war movement and the government. Just three months later, the Tet Offensive (January 1968) would prove that the war was far from over, deepening the domestic crisis and ultimately leading President Johnson to announce he would not seek re-election in March 1968.

anchor.title: Replica of Sputnik 1, First Artificial Earth Satellite (launched 1957)
anchor.creator: NSSDC / NASA (replica photographed); donor image released CC0
anchor.citation: "USSR Sputnik I, 1957, 1st Man-Made Satellite (Replica)." Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, via Wikimedia Commons (CC0), commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:USSR_Sputnik_I,_1957,_1st_Man-made_Satellite_(Replica)_(10437199454).jpg.
anchor.alt: Color photograph of a replica of Sputnik 1, the first artificial Earth satellite launched by the Soviet Union on October 4, 1957, displayed at the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum; the replica is a polished metallic sphere with four long antennas extending from it.
anchor.caption: This photograph shows a museum replica of Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite to orbit Earth, launched by the Soviet Union on October 4, 1957. The launch of Sputnik shocked the American public and triggered a crisis of confidence: if the Soviets could put a satellite in orbit, their rockets could also deliver nuclear weapons to any city in the United States. The U.S. government responded rapidly: Congress created NASA in 1958, passed the National Defense Education Act to dramatically increase funding for science and math education, and accelerated missile and space programs. The Space Race — the competition between the United States and Soviet Union to achieve superiority in space exploration — had begun. Sputnik represented a turning point in Cold War competition, demonstrating that the arms race had expanded from nuclear weapons to a global technological contest that included satellites, space exploration, education, and scientific research.

anchor.title: Opening of the Berlin Wall at Potsdamer Platz (November 1989)
anchor.creator: Staff Sergeant F. Lee Cockran / U.S. Department of Defense
anchor.citation: Cockran, F. Lee. "Opening of the Berlin Wall at Potsdamer Platz." Nov. 1989. U.S. Department of Defense (DF-ST-91-01388), via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Opening_Berlin_Wall_at_Potsdamer_Platz,_DF-ST-91-01388.jpg.
anchor.alt: Color photograph showing the opening of the Berlin Wall at Potsdamer Platz in November 1989, with jubilant crowds gathered at a breached section of the concrete Wall under bright floodlights.
anchor.caption: This photograph shows the opening of the Berlin Wall at Potsdamer Platz in November 1989 — the defining symbolic moment of the Cold War's end. The Berlin Wall, built in August 1961 to prevent East Germans from fleeing to the West, had divided Berlin for twenty-eight years and stood as the most visible symbol of the Iron Curtain separating communist Eastern Europe from democratic Western Europe. On November 9, 1989, the East German government announced citizens were free to cross, and thousands poured through checkpoints while crowds began physically tearing the Wall down. The Soviet Union, under Mikhail Gorbachev, did not send troops to stop them — a decision that confirmed the USSR was willing to let Eastern European nations chart their own futures. The Wall's fall triggered a swift chain of events: communist governments across Eastern Europe collapsed, Germany formally reunified on October 3, 1990, and the Soviet Union itself dissolved on December 25, 1991, ending the Cold War that had dominated global politics for over four decades.
